Comparisons of this game to Rocket League are inevitable but IMO a bit unfair - it's much more akin to something like Sonic Racing. But anyway, here's a lovely new game where you use a car to try to get a ball into a golf like hole by racing over fairly long circuits against human and CPU opposition. 

Like Rocket League, what seems a simple concept becomes actually quite intricate and deep once you fathom all the car control nuances and tricks. Easy to play but quite hard to master, and actually win. 

Similar to Rocket League your performance can be enhanced by pickups you earn mid-race and also rewards for achieveing certain goals, the latter of which are permanent and swappable at your bidding.

You can also be rewarded by a large range of cosmetic items which don't improve your performance at all but make you feel cooler, a bit like in Rocket League. 

Unlike Rocket League it's not so easy to find human players on the servers at the moment but that is getting better recently I see, so you'll probably have at least a couple of human players in an online game, with the rest filled by AI bots, who, unlike Rocket League do provide some challenge at first. Unlike Rocket League, there are 8 racers in a normal match. 

Playing on your own with no human competition is a bit reminiscent of Rocket League in that it might be useful practice at first but soon gets boring and is very unfulfilling. The game really relies on the competitive edge provided by other human players, in the same way that Rocket League does. 

I have to appreciate the graphics, mechanics and production values of the game, it's very nicely put together using a nice balance of cartoony graphics and physics while forcing you to feel immersed - Rocket League-like - in the coliseum of competitiveness. It definitely has that 'one more game' appeal that games like Rocket League offer, as long as you can find other players. 

So a big thumbs-up, good fun game. But as I said at the start, not really comparable to Rocket League, much more like Need for Speed Hot Pursuit.

I have played exactly one (1) multiplayer match at the time of writing this review. The parallels to Rocket League are obvious. I have great news: This does not play like a Rocket League clone, it does not feel like all it's trying to be is Rocket League. 

This game, somehow, feels like legitimately playing golf with a rocket car. Bunkers and rough actually slow your ball. The physics are weighty, the car has momentum that feels good. Controls felt great, the battle-racing aspect felt like a very comfortable and familiar backdrop to the core gameplay of just trying to get that ball in the hole. Instead of feeling like "Wish I was Playing Rocket League" this game feels distinct, fun, and unique.

Really looking forward to playing more, and strongly recommend giving this game a chance.

Turbo Golf Racing: A Fun, Fast-Paced Twist on Rocket League

Turbo Golf Racing delivers a thrilling, high-octane experience, merging the exhilarating world of golf with the fast-paced action of arcade racing. Think of it as Rocket League’s little brother with a golfing twist, and while it’s an enjoyable ride, it doesn’t quite capture the same magic that makes Rocket League an all-time classic.

Gameplay Mechanics: In Turbo Golf Racing, players control customizable vehicles equipped with a giant golf club to hit oversized balls into the goal—except this time, it’s not just about power shots. You’re racing through courses, battling rivals, and using power-ups to outmaneuver opponents while trying to get your ball into the hole first. The gameplay is fast-paced and feels like a delightful fusion of kart racing and golf, with enough chaos to keep you engaged.

Compared to Rocket League, Turbo Golf Racing keeps a similar sense of fluid, arcade-style action but shifts the primary focus from car control to the skill of hitting the ball with accuracy and timing. While Rocket League thrives on the deep mastery of aerial control and strategic positioning, Turbo Golf Racing focuses more on rapid, accessible gameplay with a slight learning curve. This makes it easier to jump into, but it might not have the same long-term depth that players love in Rocket League’s competitive scene.

Graphics and Aesthetic: Visually, Turbo Golf Racing leans into a vibrant, cartoonish aesthetic. The bright colors and whimsical environments give the game a fun, approachable feel. You’re racing through wild and imaginative golf courses with various environments—from tropical beaches to futuristic cities. It’s visually pleasing, but it doesn’t quite match the polished, almost photorealistic feel of Rocket League, which has an impressively immersive arena vibe that elevates the overall experience.

Customization: Both games offer extensive vehicle customization, but Turbo Golf Racing gives you more freedom with your car’s design. From skins to wheels to even the golf clubs used for hitting the ball, there’s plenty to personalize. Rocket League, on the other hand, excels in making customizations feel meaningful and integrated into the competitive experience with specific items that appeal to players’ skill and status.

Competitive Scene: Here’s where the comparison feels a bit uneven. Rocket League has built a massive competitive community over the years, with esports tournaments, professional leagues, and a deep tactical element that makes it a serious game for the pros. Turbo Golf Racing is more casual, focusing on fun and fast matches rather than deep strategy and positioning. While it has the potential for competitive play, it currently lacks the same level of seriousness and depth that Rocket League players crave.

Fun Factor: The real strength of Turbo Golf Racing lies in its fun factor. It’s easy to pick up and play, offering a more casual and less intense experience compared to Rocket League. If you’re looking for a lighthearted, fast-paced title to enjoy with friends, Turbo Golf Racing does its job brilliantly. However, it doesn’t quite have the same addictive quality that keeps Rocket League players coming back for more. Rocket League’s blend of skill, tactics, and team play keeps it fresh year after year, whereas Turbo Golf Racing feels more like a great way to kill time than a game that will develop a massive competitive scene of its own.

Conclusion: In the end, Turbo Golf Racing is a delightful, arcade-style racing experience with a unique twist on golf. It’s a fun game that will undoubtedly entertain, especially for players looking for a casual and enjoyable racing experience. However, if you’re comparing it directly to Rocket League, Turbo Golf Racing may feel a bit like a simplified version of its more polished and competitive counterpart. While it has its own charm and potential, it doesn’t yet have the same level of depth or esports appeal that Rocket League has so masterfully cultivated over the years.

Its hard to start a review of Turbo Golf Racing without instantly comparing it to Rocket League. Its obvious that the art style, environmental design, vehicles, cosmetics, and general 'hit the ball with vehicles that have advanced aerial controls' gameplay is trying [i]so[/i] hard to capture that same audience. However, I think there is enough deviation from the 'Rocket League formula' that makes this game stand out well on its own.

Basically, you vs others are racing to get your golf ball in the hole as quick as possible. There are a good amount of variation in the tracks, with high elevation changes and multiple routes to go through. There are also power-ups that can be used to benefit you or hurt your opponents, whether you equip them or pick them up on track. The game is also refined enough that its much more worth it's price vs other early access games. It does still need more work, with its sound design and music being its current weakest point.

So, if you are just looking for a game similar to Rocket League, you aren't going to find it here as this is car golf, not car soccer. However, if you ever wished that Rocket League had a racing mode, this game is for you. I'm hoping this game sees a resurgence once its out of early access, because its just [i]that[/i] fun.

Overall, this is a great basis for this game that [b]needs[/b] some polishing. I will preface this by mentioned I got the game through the Jingle Jam 2023 bundle, meaning my view on the game is not based on it's full price on Steam [i](currently at £14.99)[/i], hence why I have marked this review as having received the product for free.

[h2][b][u]Firstly, the positives[/u][/b][/h2]
[olist]
[*]It has elements that will appeal to both casual [b]and[/b] competitive players
[*]The 1v1 golf gamemode [i](currently a beta in the game at the time of review)[/i] is really fun and unique
[*]Yes, it is like Rocket League but golf [i](a positive because that's a good game, why not be like it where you can?)[/i]
[/olist]

[h2][b][u]The dreaded negatives[/u][/b][/h2]
[olist]
[*]Physics - This is the big one for me. It's inconstant across maps and materials on the field. It makes sense for different materials to affect your ball differently, but things like the rough are much gripper on some maps than others, without much of an obvious reason as to why
[*]Low player count - this isn't the end of the world, but it really is something to keep in mind. There isn't much to do solo, and there isn't a couch co-op mode [i](as far as I can tell)[/i], and this can lead to you feeling a bit stuck in a queue for a game for a while
[/olist]

It's important to remember that, for me, these negatives aren't 100% deal breakers, but they might be to you if you have to pay full price for the game in its current state. There's a lot of potential here, and I will continue to follow it closely [i](hence why I am recommending the game)[/i], but it is important to keep in mind the state of the game for your purchase.

This game is like [b]Rocket League meets golfing.[/b] The concept is much more fun in comparison to its competitor, IMO. However, the game isn't without its flaws. I put 8 hours into this game so here are some of my thoughts.

[b]Pros:[/b]

➤ As I already mentioned, the concept is pretty unique, fun and addictive
➤ The mechanics are easy to learn but hard to master, also they are somewhat more complex than in Rocket League, making the game all that much more interesting
➤ Varied vehicle customazation
➤ A lot of active and passive skills you can equip
➤ Great amount of maps
➤ Active updates
➤ Free battle pass
➤ Decent achievements worth grinding for
➤ In-game mission which keep you coming back

[b]Neither:[/b]

➤ The playerbase is small, you tend to play with the same people over and over again, most of the matches therefore are filled with half bots but the queue times are short, meaning you don't need to wait usually more than a minute
➤ In the first hour you kinda get to know everything about this game but you can always improve when it comes down to your skills (for some it gets repetitive real quick)

[b]Cons:[/b]

➤ There are a very few game modes you can choose from (solo = time trial, more players/bots = casual + ranked)
➤ Uncertain future, due to the small playerbase, I can see the game dying in the near future. Most likely, I see the game going free-to-play (the fact, the game was already bundled just makes my theory all that more plausible)
➤ No voice chat (it doesn't matter since there are no teammodes, still it would be a nice thing to have and let those, who don't want it, simply mute it in the settings)

[b]To sum it up,[/b] it's worth giving this game a try. After all, the game is still in early access. I had the chance of trying a demo during Steam's next fest and it was, hands down, one of the best games I tried. Maybe wait for a bit. 

I have my [b]doubts[/b] about the future of this game as I said above and even though the game seems to be getting updated regularly, it's mostly new maps and cosmetics, there doesn't seem to have been any new gamemodes or any groundbreaking updates since the game was released to the public.

I recommend this game on its merits as a game, but as a prospective buyer if you want great online multiplayer games, those days are gone. You can’t get that anymore. You honestly hardly could at any point.[/b]

The easy comparison is Rocket League, and it’s not a bad one. While the cars are similar, the depth of air gameplay is not. The cars are much [i]floatier[/i] for lack of a better term, and I think it makes for general play [u]less satisfying[/u] than Rocket League. I don’t think this means the gameplay is necessarily bad, though. Rocket League is a near untouchable gold standard for this type of control and satisfaction, so coming up short is not the worst indictment.

That said, alternative/future sports game need very tight, responsive gameplay in order to succeed. Turbo Golf Racing’s gameplay is good, and provides lots of [i]party[/i] type fun, but it’s not the competitive feeling that will engage people for addictive hours, and is necessary for competitive online multiplayer games to have staying power.

Turbo Golf Racing comes with the issue that several other games in this genre have had as well. It segments players too much by having both a ranked and casual queue (which you cannot queue for simultaneously).

It used to fill you in with bots after not so long, but very recently I tried playing some more and was in queue for over 10 minutes without getting a bot filled game, so the game is even harder to play than it was before.

The courses are fun, and although there are a lot of them, substantive differences are lacking between many. The powerups I don’t think needed to be unlocked in this way, having some kind of pseudo-progression which isn’t appropriate for a game of this type, but they do add different and creative approaches to the gameplay itself.

Overall, Turbo Golf Racing is a game I quite respect and enjoy, but I’ve not even spent that much time on it and I hardly will anymore because sadly the core feature of competitive online gameplay has already been lost to time and engagement.

Alas, the alternative/future sports game genre still awaits another top hit…

Turbo Golf Racing is very simple, especially in this state of Early Access with 30 courses available for solo play.  These are divided into three sets of ten holes, which you must complete within a set time limit.  There are three time goals for each hole, each rewarding a star for finishing under that time, and your access to additional holes is unlocked by earning stars in previous holes.  At the time of this review, I have two stars on every hole, which is basically required to access/complete all 30 holes.  Going back and earning that third star is a challenge I look forward to in my future spare time.

But all of this solo play is mere practice for the online golf game that awaits once you have learned how to play golf with a fancy sports car or truck.  Vehicle choice is limited for now, but you do unlock new vehicles through normal level-up progression. Regardless of your finishing position you will still earn XP and Gears during each match; the former increasing your level and earning you a prize at each tier, while the latter is used as currency for the in-game store where you can buy visual upgrades for your car, ball, and other flashy effects.  While not as vast as the parts selection in Rocket League, at least in Turbo Golf Racing you are actually earning “real stuff” and not silly blueprints that only unlock the privilege of buying later with real money.

Nearly all of the upgrades are visual in nature; a new paint job, a flashy spoiler, or a dangerous looking plow for the front of the vehicle to knock the ball around.  Some upgrades (Cores) do offer limited performance boosts, but these are nicely balanced with their own negative effects; like increasing your boost speed at the cost of slowing down how fast the meter refills.  Basically, the entire game is about the skill of the player and not the capabilities of the car, but it is still fun to mix and match up to two Cores per vehicle and see how it affects your game.

Controls are pretty excellent, at least when playing with a gamepad, and Turbo Golf Racing “feels” exactly like Rocket League with the same turbo, e-brake, drift, and jump mechanics.  There are fun “secrets” to figure out like getting a boost off the starting line or flipping your car to create a momentary shield to protect from a rocket attack.  The game does require more precision than Rocket League.  In that game you just hit the ball in the general direction of the net and there was a chance it would go in.  Here, you are going to need to hit the ball 20-30 times or more just to get it to the hole, so each shot needs to be accurate otherwise you end up chasing the ball around...

TGR is another multiplayer focused arcade racing game where the goal is to get your ball in the hole sooner than the rest. While the essence is simple, everything wrapped around this idea makes the game such a joy to play. There are tons of maps with their own gimmicks, plenty of skills to equip, tons of visual customisation options, a lot of in-game activities to focus on for individual progress, different game modes and most of the achievements encourage participation instead of beating others all the time. There is also a decent single player mode where all the maps can be attempted in time trial, including getting up to 3 stars. All of this content is delivered with beautiful graphics and smooth controls. I especially love being able to fly with a car whenever I want and it just feels great. In terms of finding matches, I got 9 out of 10 without caring about being online at busy times, with the European time zone at least. Even though steamdb often shows low activity, the game is carried by game pass users and the rest of the slots are filled by bots. There were a few rare moments where I encountered 4-6 out of 8 slots being real players. Most of the players were of casual-average skill level. You don’t get the sense that the community is too competitive or the sweaty type and it honestly feels great to just enjoy a multiplayer online game on your own terms.

It’s remarkable how polished and bug free the game feels even though you can tell that support was pulled sooner than expected. The golf game modes are the most recent additions and they don’t have any achievements, same can be applied to the last maps released for time trials compared to other maps. This can be seen as a good thing since you’re not forced to spend more time on the game if you don’t want to as a completionist. I’m a bit less forgiving on the game’s balance and 3 specific achievements. The game has a couple of item pickups including two types of rockets, but rockets don’t feel needed as most of the players are focused on getting their balls to the goal. It would have been easy to ignore them if there wasn’t an achievement to shield yourself from 50 rocket attacks. It might not sound like much but I only got 11 naturally in 20 hours because most don’t use it. It isn’t helped that temporary shield is a bit finicky sometimes, a proper shield is dropped randomly and there aren’t enough pickups for bigger maps. The 2 other achievements require you to be in a party lobby with 2-4 players total and start a race. I got extremely lucky to have found a public party lobby with 3 other players. It’s a shame to have those 2 achievements when the rest of the achievements could easily be gotten by joining the default race mode and focus on individual goals such as getting your ball through boost rings x amount of times etc.

You can tell the game was made with care. It’s in a good state despite it not receiving anymore updates. It might not have a long life as an online focused game but it’s a lot of fun and it feels relatively easier to find matches in this game compared to other online games with a small community I have experienced. I got the game through Humble Choice and I was fearing that most of the achievements would be annoying. It wasn’t like that for the most part luckily. The normal price is less than €10 and it’s worth it if you’re willing to enjoy it while it lasts or you weren’t planning on sticking around for long to begin with.

I thoroughly enjoy Rocket League and the game of golf. For years, myself and friends had talked about Rocket League game modes that should become a thing. Years later, lo and behold: they did it! A rocket car golf game, that's fun! Well done, and addicting.

To preface this review let me say I have over 1000hrs in Rocket League. Now to me this game is great, but suddenly I can't find a full match outside of peak hours only a couple weeks after launch. I can't put my finger on why people don't like this game honestly. I will say that this game is probably more for fans of Mario Kart than fans of Rocket League. RL is marketed as a much more competitive experience whereas the experience you will get in this game is far more casual and arcade-y. The driving is not great but it's serviceable, don't expect to be doing anything fancy like you would in RL, for example front flipping in this game only restores your boost bar so you can boost more on the ground. Being in the air slows you down so 99% of the time you want to just be driving in straight lines keeping your boost high.

Most of the complaints I see people sharing about this game is that when directly compared to RL the driving feels less intuitive, which I agree with. I also think about how chaotic and hard to control the physics can be in RL and it makes me appreciate that the ball in this game feels and acts more like a golf ball. Turbo Golf Racing is a fantastic game that I admittedly would never have tried if not for the free weekend that was running when I purchased. This game is heavily compared to rocket league which is honestly not my thing.

The reviews that compare this game to rocket league are a little off in my opinion. Sure, you are driving a car, hitting a ball. But the similarities pretty much end there. Turbo golf is mostly a time trial type game. You can shoot rockets at your opponents but there is no collision with other players or their balls. Your score is purely based on your performance, even if playing in a group. The party system is just to ensure you get into the same match as your friends.

There is a ton of customisation in this game with a whole heap of different parts to customise the look of your car, as well as power cores to let you activate abilities to help complete the courses. The season progression is nowhere near as grindy as other games, even ones where the season pass is paid. No buying a battle pass with this game each season has been free and I don't see that changing. With playing for the free play weekend and playing casually for a couple of weeks I completed it no problem. Probably 10 hours max.

The one downfall of Turbo Golf Racing is the low player base. You can still get into matches as they fill the spots with bots after a couple of minutes of waiting. Generally you will be up against 2-4 other players and the rest of the slots (8 "players" per match) will be filled by bots. I only play casual matches so playing bots doesn't bother me. However, ranked play can be an issue for some with a the low pop.

Overall I would say this game is definitely worth a try. You will know if it's for you within the two hour refund window for sure.

Turbo Golf Racing is a title I played on Game Pass, in playing it again, I remember it is a solid idea, take car sports and make it work for Golf.  Here you try to hit a large ball into the cup.  Rather than worry about strokes, this is purely a race to see who can do it the fastest, and with interesting abilities and courses, the experience works… at first. 

The problem with Turbo Golf Racing is there are not enough courses to the point that I saw repetition after only thirty minutes of playing online.  The single-player offerings are only basic time trials and while there are missions, none of them will take too long.  The player base is a bit dead as well.  I believe the game uses bots, signified by the gears on screen, but I was usually finding a match with between three to five real players, and the bots would almost always finish last.   Rocket League succeeded by having a single course and forcing players to master it and the controls.  Turbo Golf Racing has just enough courses and not enough players that there’s probably never going to be the level of competition here. 

Pick this up if you want to play an interesting Golf game for half an hour or so.  After about thirty minutes I remember why I didn’t go too deep with this title, and while this is on the third season and still in Early Access, even with DLC already, this is really just a grindy experience before long, and the levels are interesting the first time, but hardly something I wanted to play for hours, especially with how often the same ones come around.

This has the makings of a cool game but it just isn't fun yet. People are saying it's like Rocket League x Golf With Your Friends, but it misses an important thing that those two games have in common: player interaction. GWYF is about playing in small groups and then accidentally (on purpose) trolling each other by colliding your balls. RL is about close-knit teamplay and direct competition: you're playing with some people (possibly friends) against some other people (possibly also friends, since you can set up custom games). In Turbo Golf Racing you can't collide with other players' cars or balls, like TrackMania, so the only player interaction is with the one "homing missle" weapon, which you don't pick up that frequently, there's no interesting gameplay around, and it just slows someone down by a few seconds. There's also no custom games, you can just join a party with friends to get into the same match.

Obviously full player-on-player collision would lead to a lot of trolling, with troll players not even playing their own ball and just knocking opponents off the map, but even ball-to-ball collision would be more interaction and make that kind of trolling a lot harder; and a custom game mode where you can turn on collisions would allow you to get the GWYF trolling experience with your party without ruining the public games. After that I'd like to see more gameplay options explored to allow more player interaction and competition.

Finally, the car's movement and controls just don't feel as fluid and controllable as RL, particularly the double-jump flipping. Right now, I think the silly game modes they keep putting as short-term events in RL are much more fun than this, but I do have high hopes that this game will find its fun in the next six months to a year.

Game is officially out, and here is my final review.

Single player: The solo time trials are super fun and a great time kill that might make it worth buying the game. The controls are smooth, the maps are cleanly laid out, and there is enough variation to keep you busy for a while. It's not too hard to 3-star every map if you practice it a few times, but some are going to be easier than others. The game-play is designed around "cores" that give you different abilities that can influence your play-style on each map. Find which cores work best for you, and tackle the time trial.

Multiplayer-Golf Mode: The golf multiplayer is a pretty cool and is what you would think of when first coming into this game. Some of the maps can take forever to complete, but it's a pretty solid concept. This isn't the main play-style of the game, but it was still a cool addition.

Multiplayer-Golf Racing: This is the part of the game that warranted me not recommending it. I have complained, as have many others, that the match-making for the game is absolute garbage. You will continually get matched with players that are really outside your skill-level, and there isn't anything you can do about it. New players try out the game, get their ass kicked by people who have played this game non-stop for a year, then they give up after realizing how out-matched they are against most of the player base. A large portion of the ranked community isn't comprised of new players, they are legacy players that have been grinding the game for over a year. This is frustrating, because in my opinion this is going to be the death of the game and has been my biggest complaint. I really though after seeing what the ranked playlist devolved into pre-1.0 a change would be made, but I was wrong.

Community: The community for the game is a cringy cult, and I would avoid the discord server. Not only is it a very "clicky" community, they are very toxic and aggressive to people who don't play how they want. If I am in a game I know I am not going to win, you know what I do? I leave. The point of a game is to have fun, right? You know what isn't fun? Being forced to play out a 5-hole series against somebody that is going to inevitably beat you. Just leave, accept the penalty, and hope to god you get matched with more even competition. Most of these toxic people rage if you leave(and I even received a few...colorful DM's), because you refused to stay in a game. I don't get the anger, because they still get the win and the points.

Not here to try and convince anybody that TGR isn't worth their time.. doubt with a Steam population as low as it has, barely anyone will even see this. Still, I left couple lengthier feedback posts on TGR discord for the devs past season, and wanted to see if Season 2 brings any welcome changes - not seeing any, so I'll lay down the truth here as well.

This should not have been an online requirement live service game. I think the devs thought this would be some big hit to take on bigger giants in the market, and instead it just dwindles in its very low playerbase, making the online part of the game (one that earns all the fancy cosmetics) a real chore - long and ridiculously unfair matchmaking (whilst not even filling up most spots in a match) ; brutally grindy season track (exponential curve, so first 10 levels is like one last) ; and a lot of cores and every single cosmetic tied to online progression only, so if you want to have fun by yourself trying to do better on some tracks solo (whilst looking fly), then be willing to invest a bunch of time into playing with others just to get bombarded by missles every 5 seconds, trying to finish some dumb daily missions like a good little sucker. 

Can't just have a fun game, no no no - got to have that seasonal track and daily logins, to keep the player retention like every other BS live service game, right?!

First season took me approx 50 hours to finish, and I had a winrate of over 50% over 327 matches (games should fill up with 8 players, but most of the matches it was me vs 1-5 other players, making 6-8 player lobbies very rare, and I did try both NA/EU servers at all kinds of different times.. after a few weeks into the season the waiting time (matchmaking > loading players/levels > flyby cam > potg) takes up as much time as actually going through the 3 maps in one match, so by that conclusion a single season will waste tens of hours of your time, just by mindlessly waiting around.

As mentioned, the player count is kind of low (not screaming the game is dying.. but expect some queue times go upwards of 2-5 minutes further into the season). Steamdb shows around ~20 people playing (it was around 60-100 when the first season launched), so most of the players come from this game being a freebie on Game Pass, so if that contract ever ends (which they usually eventually do), expect the player count to totally plummet. To make things worse, there are 6-7 regions to play in (good for latency, but terrible for a very low population in online games, forcing segregation).

Also this game is centered around online-only, so if TGR crew doesn't have a end-of-life plan for this game, it can just shut down over the next year or so with the usual "oh well we tried, but we're so glad to have people come along on this journey (but this aint profitable for us anymore so we're shutting down)" type of bs as usual. I hope I'm very wrong about this, but TGR does not have any client-saves, nor can this be played in offline mode, even if you're just interested in solo-ing some tracks for better times or to have simple casual fun. And to top it all off, this will be another one of those infinitely in Early Access type of games, to justify whatever is wrong with it - and all the diehard fans can always make excuses "oh well its still beta" or "oh, this is planned to be implemented sometime / soon / who knows" like any of it matters if the game is already in full motion with selling itself and pumping out seasons.

To touch on cosmetics, this game goes hard on exclusivity, so hey.. if you didn't play in Beta / Season 1 / Season X, then feel ready to see others with stuff you'll never own, because clearly you're not worthy to be with the cool crowd. As far as other games doing seasonal track better, Minecraft Dungeons has a way to let people progress whatever season pass they choose for those rewards, but I guess 'fear of missing out' is better to keep people active from season to season. 

Also the store, for no good reason at all, rotates out items daily (and some smaller stuff every 6 hours).. So, why does that matter? Again, purely for suckering people into logging in daily, so if you're after an item to come back into rotation that you weren't able to afford (or missed out) when it was last in, be ready to log in daily for 2-3 months with your fingers crossed (quite literally that was the time for something I wanted in Season 1 to come back) - all of the cosmetics governed by 'you playing vs others' (something that this game doesn't even feel to mention on its store page).. if you buy the game, you get no cosmetics apart from one base car. More stuff added in these little rotations also mean less likelyhood of you ever seeing them again.

Still no cosmetic presets either, and there's already a decent amount of items in the game that this should have been long implemented (should've simply done one loadout for each car body), but its not like anybody plays this game for the cosmetics anyway, right? RIGHT?!

There are a bunch of other smaller issues as well, but I doubt the devs decided to consider my feedback on their discord (which is actually nicely done for this game), and I doubt they will consider anything mentioned here either. I don't hate the game, but I do despise the GaaS model they decided to tie this game onto and then sink it. It plays fine and was fun at first, but personally I'd suggest investing your time into Rocket League instead, if hitting balls with cars is your thing - as terrible and toxic as that game can be, at least you can still get better at it after playing over 10 hours, and it will probably be around in the coming years - something I can't see TGR have a future for (and I do hope I'm wrong).

Sadly, if/once I'll be back to complete S2, I won't care for player competition in it, and will just have to idle-macro my PC for those cosmetic rewards for 3-4 days straight, whilst I play some other game that is fun and values my time.
